title: Variable Scope
body:
**Where** in the program text a name is visible. A compile-time question, answered by looking
at braces.

C++ is block scoped: a [[Variable]] is visible from its declaration to the closing `}` of the
block it was declared in, and in every block nested inside that one.

```c++
int g = 1;              // global scope: whole file

void f() {
	int a = 2;          // function scope
	for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
		int b = 3;      // block scope: this loop only
	}
	// b is not in scope here. i is not either.
	// g and a are.
}
```

Declaring the loop counter in the `for` header keeps it inside the loop, which is what you
want; declaring it above the loop leaks it into the rest of the function.

**Shadowing**: an inner declaration with the same name hides the outer one for the length of
the block. Legal, and almost always a mistake.

Scope is the pair to [[Variable Lifetime]] and they are constantly confused:

| | Scope | Lifetime |
|---|---|---|
| Question | *where* is the name visible | *when* does the storage exist |
| Decided | at compile time, by braces | at run time |
| Tool | reading the code | knowing the [[Storage Class]] |

They come apart in both directions. A `static` local is out of scope between calls but its
storage never goes away. Heap memory from `new` has no name at all after the [[Pointer]] to it
goes out of scope, and it still exists, which is a memory leak.

The design argument: keep scope as small as it will go. A name visible everywhere is a name
anything can change, which is the first-year version of the global-variable case in
[[Coupling and Cohesion]]. Local variables are also why [[Function]]s compose at all, since
two functions can both use `i` without colliding.
